paragraphs: Fyodor Pavlovitch, by the way, had been away from our town for some time before this. Three or four years after his wife died, he went off to the south of Russia and eventually turned up in Odessa, where he spent several years. At first, as he put it, he got to know “a lot of low Jews, Jewesses, and Jewkins,” and he ended up being welcomed by “Jews high and low alike.” We may suppose that it was in this period that he developed a peculiar knack for making money and hoarding it. He came back to our town for good only three years before Alyosha arrived. His old acquaintances found him terribly aged, though he was by no means an old man. He carried himself not exactly with more dignity, but with more effrontery. The old buffoon now had an insolent itch to turn other people into buffoons. His depravity with women was not merely what it had been, but even more revolting. In a short time he opened a great number of new taverns in the district. It was plain that he had perhaps a hundred thousand roubles, or not much less. Many people in the town and the district were soon in his debt, and had put up good security, naturally. Lately, too, he looked somehow bloated. He seemed more irresponsible and more erratic, and had sunk into a sort of incoherence: he would start one thing and go on with another, as though he were letting himself go altogether. He got drunk more and more often. And without that same servant Grigory, who by then had aged a good deal himself, and who sometimes looked after him almost like a tutor, Fyodor Pavlovitch might have landed in terrible scrapes. Alyosha’s arrival seemed to touch even his moral side, as though something that had long been dead in his soul had woken up in this prematurely old man.

“Do you know,” he often said, looking at Alyosha, “you’re like her, ‘the crazy woman’”—that was what he called his dead wife, Alyosha’s mother. It was Grigory who showed Alyosha the “crazy woman’s” grave. He took him to our town cemetery and pointed out, in a remote corner, a cast-iron tombstone, cheap but decently kept. It bore the name and age of the dead woman and the date of her death, with a four-line verse underneath, the sort commonly seen on old-fashioned middle-class graves. To Alyosha’s amazement, the tomb turned out to be Grigory’s doing. He had put it up over the poor “crazy woman’s” grave at his own expense, after Fyodor Pavlovitch, whom he had often pestered about the grave, left for Odessa and abandoned both the grave and all his memories. Alyosha showed no particular emotion at the sight of his mother’s grave. He just listened to Grigory’s detailed and solemn account of how the tomb was built, stood there with his head bowed, and walked away without a word. It was perhaps a year before he went to the cemetery again. But this little episode had an effect on Fyodor Pavlovitch—and a very original one. He suddenly took a thousand roubles to our monastery to pay for requiems for his wife’s soul. Not for the second wife, Alyosha’s mother, the “crazy woman,” though, but for the first, Adelaïda Ivanovna, the one who used to thrash him. That same evening he got drunk and ran down the monks to Alyosha. He was far from religious himself; he had probably never set so much as a penny candle in front of a saint’s image. Strange surges of sudden feeling and sudden thought are common in men of that type.

I have already said that he looked bloated. His face by now carried unmistakable marks of the life he had led. There were long fleshy bags under his small eyes, which were always insolent, suspicious, and ironical, and a mass of deep wrinkles in his little fat face. His Adam’s apple hung below his sharp chin like a great fleshy goiter, which gave him a peculiar, repulsive, sensual look. On top of that came a long, rapacious mouth with full lips, and between them you could see little stumps of black, rotten teeth. He slobbered whenever he began to speak. He enjoyed making jokes about his own face, though I believe he was quite pleased with it. He liked above all to point to his nose, which was not very large, but very fine and noticeably hooked. “A regular Roman nose,” he would say, “and with my goiter I look just like an ancient Roman patrician of the decadent period.” He seemed proud of it.

Soon after visiting his mother’s grave, Alyosha suddenly announced that he wanted to enter the monastery, and that the monks were ready to accept him as a novice. He explained that he wanted this very much, and that he was solemnly asking for his father’s consent. The old man knew that the elder Zossima, who lived in the monastery’s hermitage, had made a special impression on his “gentle boy.”

“Well, he’s the most honest monk of the lot, of course,” he remarked, after listening to Alyosha in thoughtful silence, and seeming hardly surprised at the request. “H’m!... So that’s where you want to be, my gentle boy?”

He was half drunk, and suddenly he broke into his slow, half-drunken grin, which had a bit of cunning and tipsy slyness in it. “H’m!... I had a feeling you’d end up in something like this. Would you believe it? You were making straight for it. Well, of course you have your own two thousand. That’s a dowry for you. And I’ll never desert you, my angel. I’ll pay whatever they need for you there, if they ask. But if they don’t ask, why should we bother them? What do you say? You know, you spend money like a canary, two grains a week. H’m!... Do you know that near one monastery there’s a place outside the town where every baby knows that nobody lives but ‘the monks’ wives,’ as they’re called? Thirty women, I believe. I’ve been there myself. You know, it’s interesting in its own way, of course, as a change. The trouble is, it’s awfully Russian. No French women there. Of course they could get them fast enough, they’ve got plenty of money. If word gets out, they’ll turn up. Well, here there’s nothing of the sort, no ‘monks’ wives,’ and two hundred monks. They’re honest. They keep the fasts. I’ll admit it.... H’m.... So you want to be a monk? And do you know, I’m sorry to lose you, Alyosha; would you believe it, I’ve really got fond of you? Well, it’s a good chance. You’ll pray for us sinners; we’ve sinned too much here. I’ve always wondered who would pray for me, and whether there’s anyone in the world who would. My dear boy, I’m awfully stupid about that. You wouldn’t believe it. Awfully. You see, stupid as I am about it, I keep thinking, I keep thinking—now and then, of course, not all the time. I can’t imagine, I think, that the devils would forget to drag me down to hell with their hooks when I die. Then I wonder—hooks? Where would they get them? What from? Iron hooks? Where do they forge them? Have they got some sort of foundry down there? The monks in the monastery probably believe there’s a ceiling in hell, for instance. Now, I’m ready to believe in hell, but without a ceiling. That makes it more refined, more enlightened, more Lutheran, that is. And after all, what difference does it make whether it has a ceiling or not? But there’s a damnable question hidden in it, you know? If there’s no ceiling, there can be no hooks, and if there are no hooks, the whole thing collapses, which is unlikely too, because then nobody would drag me down to hell, and if they don’t drag me down, where’s the justice in the world? _Il faudrait les inventer_, those hooks, on purpose for me alone, because if you only knew, Alyosha, what a blackguard I am.”
“But there are no hooks there,” Alyosha said, looking at his father gently and seriously.

“Yes, yes, only the shadows of hooks, I know, I know. That’s how a Frenchman described hell: ‘_J’ai vu l’ombre d’un cocher qui avec l’ombre d’une brosse frottait l’ombre d’une carrosse._’ How do you know there are no hooks, darling? Once you’ve lived with the monks, you’ll change your tune. But go and find out the truth there, and then come and tell me. Anyway, it’s easier to go to the other world if you know what’s there. Besides, it’ll be more fitting for you with the monks than here with me, a drunken old man, and young harlots ... though you’re like an angel, nothing touches you. I expect nothing will touch you there either. That’s why I’m letting you go, because I hope so. You’ve got all your wits about you. You’ll burn, and you’ll burn out; you’ll be healed and come back again. And I’ll wait for you. I feel you’re the only creature in the world who hasn’t condemned me. My dear boy, I feel it, you know. I can’t help feeling it.”
And he actually started blubbering. He was sentimental. He was wicked and sentimental.
